teaser.en: A flowering plant that lives its whole life underwater, it feeds dugongs and shelters the fish that Digo fishers catch.

summary.en: Narrowleaf seagrass is a true flowering plant that lives fully submerged in the sea, forming meadows on the intertidal sand flats. These meadows feed dugongs and turtles and shelter the fish, octopus and sea cucumbers on which coastal fishing depends.

about.en:
Despite its name, seagrass is not a seaweed. It is a flowering plant, with roots, leaves and tiny flowers, that has adapted to living completely underwater. Narrowleaf seagrass has very thin, flat, ribbon-like leaves, only a millimetre or two wide, growing from creeping stems buried in the sand.

Where it grows thickly, it forms soft green meadows that sway in the current.

where.en: It grows on the intertidal sand flats, where it is often exposed at the lowest tides. Seagrass meadows fringe Gazi Bay, Diani-Chale and Vanga-Shimoni. Walk out across the flats at a spring low tide and you will see it carpeting the sand in shallow pools.

uses.en: Seagrass meadows are nurseries and feeding grounds for the fish and animals that Digo fishers depend on: rabbitfish, parrotfish, octopus and sea cucumbers. The meadows also trap sediment, keeping the water clear and helping to protect beaches.

names.en: No Digo name has been recorded yet. Swahili speakers usually call sea plants in general *mwani*. In English it is narrowleaf seagrass, and its scientific name is *Halodule uninervis*.

conservation.en: The seagrass meadows of Gazi Bay, Diani-Chale and Vanga-Shimoni are feeding grounds for dugongs, green turtles and rabbitfish, and nurseries for young fish. This is a favoured dugong food.

reason.en: Same family (Cymodoceaceae), grows in the same meadows
